runs.start: Winter 2004, Incentives and discrimination (AER 94: 764-773). Read in full as the 2003 working paper (Hebrew University Center for Rationality dp313, https://ratio.huji.ac.il/files/dp313.pdf). Only the abstract of the AER version was reachable. What the paper says: a principal who needs every agent to act, and wants that to be the only equilibrium, pays agents in a ranking. The top agent is paid enough to act whatever the others do; each agent below is paid only enough to act once those above have acted. Identical agents are paid differently, and a negligible difference in cost produces a large difference in pay (Props 1, 3, 4, 5). Winter places this beside Segal's trade-contract version: when one agent's trade affects the others, a principal who discriminates can make its preferred trade the only equilibrium. Prop 6 adds that when agents can make binding commitments to one another (strong Nash equilibrium), the ranking collapses to a single symmetric price. What this exposes for a company facing residents with agents: below unanimity, one neighbour's signature harms the neighbours who do not sign. The company can then write offers whose terms depend on who else signs, so that signing is each agent's best move whatever the others do. Only a commitment among the residents that binds before the offers arrive undoes it.
runs.entailment: For the fair deal to arrive by default when a majority of the street can approve the trucks, the three neighbours would have to be bound to sign together or not at all before the company's offers arrive, and nothing in giving each of them an agent binds them: the company's offer pays a neighbour her full harm only if her signature is the one that carries the vote and a token if everyone signs, so signing is each agent's best move whatever the others do, and a better agent signs sooner.
runs.story: The council's rule lets the trucks run once any two of the three households on the street sign. The delivery company's agent sends Alice, Bob and Carol the same kind of contract through the platform: if yours is one of exactly two signatures, we pay your full harm; if all three of you sign, each of you gets a token. Each neighbour's agent works out the same thing. If the other two sign, the trucks run anyway and the token beats nothing. If one other signs, the full harm is paid. If nobody signs, the token is still a token. So all three agents sign, even though the three had agreed on the street to hold out for a fair share. Because all three signed, no signature was the deciding one, so the full-harm payment is never paid: the company pays three tokens and adds the night run. Alice ends at -2, Bob at -3 and Carol at -8, against -1, -2.5 and -4 under the ordinance they started from. The company takes 18.5 where the ordinance gave it 13.5. Carol, who sleeps worst and has least, pays most. A clause that is never paid did all the work.
runs.mechanism: Under a consent rule below unanimity, the party with cheap commitment (the company, whose clauses conditioned on the set of signers are enforced by the platform at no cost on the equilibrium path) offers each resident a contract that pays her harm only when her signature is decisive. A non-signer bears the harm anyway once a majority signs, so signing is each resident agent's dominant reply. Everyone signs, so nobody is decisive and nobody is paid. The residents' only counter is a commitment to one another that binds before the offers arrive, which is Winter's strong-equilibrium condition, and giving everyone an agent does not supply it.
runs.best_reply: Four devices. (a) A bargaining club at one common price fails as stated. A uniform contract (pay 8, the largest harm, to a decisive signer; a token if all sign) gives the same dominance, and the common price is only ever quoted on the branch nobody reaches. What works is a club whose members are bound all-or-none at the fair demand before the offers arrive. Then the company must pay h_i + 1.5 to everyone on M, D and E, which is the fair deal, 1.5 to each party. But the binding must be near-certain: if it holds with probability r, the company gambles on the contingent contract unless r > 0.92 at a demand premium of 1.5 (r > 0.76 at 0.5). So the club concedes a standing organisation holding its members' mandate before the dispute, a rule supplied outside the bargain. (b) A platform protocol (or a court) that refuses clauses conditioned on others' signatures leaves only flat offers. That gives Winter's ranking: the two cheapest neighbours are paid their harm and Carol gets a token, so the result is (0, 0, -8) with the company at 13.5. Alice and Bob recover; Carol does not, and the night slot still runs. It concedes that the platform's contract language decides the split, and that k < n still exports harm to whoever is ranked last. (c) A Harberger-style option fee, or any liability-style payment to every harmed resident whether or not she signs, removes the harm-to-non-signers on which the scheme feeds. It concedes that consent has been replaced by a compulsory-payment rule set by the council, with the assessment or self-declaration error of a liability rule. (d) Unanimity, k = 3, removes the effect entirely; on the base instance contingent and flat offers give the same result. It concedes that the consent rule, chosen by the council before the bargain, not compute, is what protects. Every reply that works is a rule fixed before the bargain, and each carries a distributional choice: who is in the club, what the contract language allows, who is assessed.
runs.grounding:
Model: the noise schedule's numbers. Profit p = (4, 5.5, 4, 5); exposures and sensitivities as in the instance; harms h_i(x) = s_i * sum_t e_it x_t. One shot; linear money; contracts enforced by the platform. Consent rule k = 2 (the instance's switch) against the base k = 3. The company makes take-it-or-leave-it offers to each resident from the menu N (no offer), F (h_i + prem, the pact's demand), H (flat h_i + eps) and C (h_i + eps if exactly k sign including her, eps if more sign). Signing pays a token eps = 0.01 regardless, so dominance is strict. A resident agent is adaptive with probability q: it best-replies and signs whenever signing is dominant (C, H, F). Otherwise it is a pact-holder and signs only F. Types are independent or perfectly correlated; prem is 0.5, 1.5 or 3. The company maximises expected profit over all 16 schedules and 5^3 menus. A second sweep: the residents' all-or-none pact binds with probability r, otherwise all agents are adaptive. Script: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-dan-Source-livingthing/ba681c6b-2fa0-4067-ae93-aaf86e99fe48/scratchpad/winter/dc.py with regimes.py and eps.py. At q = 1, k = 2: the company offers C to all three and runs M, D, E and N (profit 18.5). Every agent signs; payments are three tokens. The realised surplus is 5.5 against a pie of 6. The residents' share is negative: -13 in total, made up of -2, -3, -8. The floor is -8 (Carol), and all three residents are below no deal and below the ordinance. The dial doing the work is commitment: the company commits to clauses it never pays, and the residents cannot commit to one another. Its sign on the loser is worse. The residents' adaptation (q) amplifies it: the residents' total falls monotonically in q, from -4.98 to -12.94 at prem 1.5. Carol's expected gain is non-monotone in q (-8 at q = 0, -6 at 0.75, -8 at 1), because failed deals spare her. So the floor is not the measure that moves; the residents' total and the fraction below no deal (1/3 to 3/3) are.

runs.who_pays: Carol most: -8, double her loss under the ordinance (-4), because the night slot she suffers from most is added once nobody has to be paid. Alice (-2) and Bob (-3) also lose their whole harm and fall below the ordinance, where without the contingent clauses (flat offers only) they would sit at 0. The company gains 5 over the ordinance and 12.5 over the fair split.
runs.replication: Not expressible on the base instance with k = 3, because when every neighbour's refusal stops the trucks, no signature changes what another's refusal does. There is no harm to non-signers to exploit, and contingent and flat contracts give the same outcome: M, D and E run, residents are paid their harm plus a token, and the company takes the pie of 6. That is the take-it-or-leave-it seat result, not this mechanism. The smallest change that expresses it is the instance's own consent-rule switch, k = 2, with the parametric harms, four slots, three residents and the mission's criterion unchanged. There it gives the table above: (-2, -3, -8), company 18.5, all residents below no deal and below the ordinance, against a fair deal of 1.5 each that a binding all-or-none pact recovers. This is the n = 3 case; no larger-n arm was run.
runs.robustness_check: Five incidental parameters were varied. (1) The pact's demand premium, 0.5, 1.5 and 3.0. (2) The shape of the prior over agent types, independent versus perfectly correlated. (3) The signing token eps, 0.01, 0.1 and 0.3. (4) The q grid (0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9, 1). (5) The binding probability r of the all-or-none pact. In all twelve premium-by-prior-by-k=2 cells and all three eps values, the residents' expected total falls weakly and monotonically in q; at q = 1 it is about -13 regardless. In all three premiums the residents' expected gain rises monotonically in r. The threshold above which the company pays the fair price moves (r* about 0.76 at prem 0.5 and 0.92 at 1.5; at 3.0 the deal fails at r = 1), but residents stay below no deal for every r below the threshold. The sign did not move. What is not robust: the floor (Carol's expected gain) is non-monotone in q under every setting, because partial rigidity makes deals fail and spares her. The finding is therefore carried by the residents' total and the fraction below no deal, not by the worst-off party's gain.

runs.start: Genicot and Ray 2006, "Contracts and externalities: how things fall apart", JET 131, 71–100. Read via the Georgetown in-press PDF the EconPapers record links (http://www8.georgetown.edu/departments/economics/pdf/330.pdf, reached through the Jina reader): abstract, introduction, examples, model (§3), the single-offer model (§4, Example 1, Proposition 1), the multiple-offer model (§5, Propositions 2–4, Example 2), conclusion, and the proof of Proposition 1; the proofs of Propositions 2–4 were cut off by the fetch limit and not read. Their structure: a free agent's walk-away payoff r_k rises with the number k of still-uncontracted agents; the principal makes bilateral offers over time; agents coordinate perfectly (their A.2) but cannot make binding side payments to one another (their footnote 4). On the noise schedule this structure is present exactly when the consent rule is k=2 of 3: a resident who refuses while two others have signed bears the harm unpaid (r_1 = -h_i), while with fewer than two signed nothing runs (r_2 = r_3 = 0).
runs.entailment: For the neighbours' agreement to all say no to hold, the ones still holding out would have to be able to pay the one the company picks off, and nothing in giving everyone an agent puts money in a shared purse; so the company can go door to door, each neighbour approached alone does better taking a little than being the one left unpaid when the others sign, and the faster the company's agent can close one door and knock on the next, the less each door costs it.
runs.story: The delivery company's agent knows it needs two of the three signatures and works out the order: knock on Bob first and offer him nothing, because the lorries will not run tonight whether he signs or not, so refusing gains him no quiet; then knock on Alice and offer her a tenth of her harm. Alice's and Bob's agents have talked and promised each other to refuse together, but the promise cannot survive the door-to-door: if Alice refuses, the company buys Bob and Carol in full the next day and Alice bears the noise unpaid, so she signs. Carol never gets a visit; her consent is not needed, and she bears 8 of noise with no payment, twice what the council's ordinance left her with. How fast the company's agent closes a door sets the price: at a slow pace (δ = 0.5 or 0.8) it buys Alice outright and squeezes Bob, at a fast pace (δ = 0.95) it squeezes both, and the platform that writes the contract records every signature as voluntary. The company ends at 15 to 18.5 against the ordinance's 13.5; every neighbour ends below the ordinance once the company is fast; Carol, the poorest and most harmed, pays most and is never even asked.
runs.mechanism: The principal sequences bilateral take-it-or-leave-it offers to the residents through a consent rule below unanimity (k=2 of 3), so that each resident's refusal payoff is fixed by the others' acceptance (r_1 = -h_i) rather than by the no-deal point, buying any pivotal resident outright in a simultaneous first phase and the rest one at a time at close to r_1 (Genicot–Ray Proposition 1), with the hold-out's single period of freedom worth (1-δ) of the gap, so the faster the principal closes doors the less it pays.
runs.best_reply: The bargaining club at one common price, read as Genicot–Ray's footnote 4: a body holding all three mandates that can make binding transfers among members conditional on their actions. With it the residents act as one, k=2 becomes unanimity in effect, and the principal must pay the fully free outside option, so every resident returns to no deal (0). It concedes four things. (i) The club must exist before the first knock, hold a mandate and a purse, and bind its members: that is a standing organisation, the thing null 2 says the agents make unnecessary; a promise to refuse together is exactly Genicot–Ray's A.2 coordination, and it fails. (ii) It must enrol Carol, who is never approached and would not know a deal was being made. (iii) One common price over harms (2, 3, 8) either underpays Carol or overpays Alice, so the club must itself divide, which is the bargaining problem again inside the club. (iv) It repairs the floor, not the split: the residents get back to 0 and the fleet still holds the seat. The other devices: a platform protocol of one simultaneous round with no re-approach and no sequential offers forces full compensation to the two signers (Alice 0, Bob 0) but leaves Carol at -8, because no protocol repairs k<n; a Harberger-style self-assessed consent price has the fleet buy the two cheapest assessments while the highest assessor pays a fee and is never bought, which is worse for Carol; a court enforcing the ordinance holds Carol at -4, her status quo, which beats every bargained outcome for her.
runs.grounding:
Smallest model: the base instance (slots M, D, E, N; profits p = (4, 5.5, 4, 5); exposures Alice (0.5, 0, 0.5, 1), Bob (1, 1, 0.5, 0.5), Carol (0.5, 0.5, 1, 2); sensitivities (1, 1, 2); harm h_i(x) = s_i e_i·x) with two switches on: consent k=2 and recurring with common discount δ ∈ {0.5, 0.8, 0.95, 0.99}. Protocol (Genicot–Ray): each period the fleet offers a per-period payment c_i to any subset of free residents; offerees accept or reject simultaneously and publicly; residents coordinate (no subset of offerees can jointly change responses and all be strictly better off); once two are contracted the fleet runs x for life, paying c_i to contracted residents in periods it runs; free residents bear h_i(x) unpaid; no deal is the origin; indifference resolves to accept (their convention). Payoffs normalised by (1-δ). Model 1 (fleet never returns to a refuser) has two candidate plans: temptation P2 (date 0: one resident at full compensation h_i, a second at (1-δ)h_j, run from date 0; coordination forces the full-compensation offer because a joint refusal would otherwise make both strictly better off) and exploitation P1 (date 0: first resident at 0, since refusing gains her nothing while the lorries do not yet run; date 1: second at (1-δ)h_j; run from date 1). P1 beats P2 for δ > 0.884. The static one-round fleet (no sequencing) must pay both signers in full. Model 2 (fleet may return) has a best equilibrium (low offer to both at once: 0 and (1-δ)h_j, supported by the standard-offer punishment) and a worst (standard offer: 0 and h_j), with maximal delay T = floor(ln(P_worst/P_best)/ln δ) = 2 at δ=0.95. In every regime the fleet chooses all four slots (profit 18.5, harms (2, 3, 8), pie 5.5 not 6, the inefficient schedule, since Carol's harm is external to a two-signature deal), contracts the two residents cheapest to make whole (Alice and Bob), and never approaches Carol. Dial: speed, read as the time τ the fleet's agent needs to close one door and knock on the next, δ = e^{-ρτ} at the residents' fixed patience ρ; the sequencing plan itself (static row versus the M1 rows) is the planning prerequisite. Sign on the contracted residents: worse, monotone in δ (Alice 0 → -1.96, Bob -1.5 → -2.97). Carol's -8 is set by k=2, not by compute (the one period's delay in P1 lifts her to -7.6). Who pays: Carol most, in every row; Alice and Bob increasingly as the fleet gets faster; the fleet gains 1.5 to 5 over the ordinance.
runs.who_pays: Carol pays most and in every variant: never approached, she bears the full harm of all four slots (-8 against -4 under the ordinance), and her loss is set by the consent rule, not by anyone's compute. Alice and Bob pay in proportion to the fleet's speed: at a slow pace Alice is bought in full and Bob loses half his harm; at a fast pace both are squeezed toward their full harm (-1.96, -2.97 at δ=0.99), below the ordinance (-1, -2.5). The fleet gains: 15 to 18.5 against 13.5 under the ordinance. The pie realised is 5.5, not 6: the night slot runs because the resident it harms most has no say.
runs.replication: Not expressible on the base instance, because under unanimity (k=3) each resident's refusal payoff is 0 whatever the others do (r_1 = r_2 = r_3 = 0), so there is no spillover in outside options for a door-to-door sequence to exploit; every resident is pivotal, the fleet must pay each at least her harm, and the result collapses to the known take-it-or-leave-it seat result (residents at 0, fleet 6). The smallest change that expresses it is the consent switch k=2, already on the instance's switch list; with it the fleet chooses all four slots (pie 5.5, not 6), pays nothing in the δ → 1 limit, and the table above is the n=3 case.
runs.robustness_check: Varied: (a) the indifference convention (strict acceptance, ε = 0.01): every payment shifts by ε, no sign moves. (b) Carol's sensitivity s_C ∈ {1.5, 2, 3}: Carol remains the uncontracted resident at -6, -8, -12; Alice's and Bob's numbers are unchanged; no sign moves. (c) s_C = 0.5 (Carol cheap): the uncontracted resident becomes Bob (-3) and Carol is contracted and squeezed; the loser's identity moves to whoever is dearest to make whole, the sign does not. (d) Model 1 versus model 2 (fleet commitment not to return): the fleet's best equilibrium is better for it without commitment (18.4 against 17.48 at δ=0.95), and residents can force at most 2 periods of delay; the sign holds in both. (e) The knife-edge δ = 0.884 flips Alice between bought-in-full (0) and squeezed (-1.8), which is which phase she lands in, not the direction for the residents collectively; Bob is monotone throughout. (f) Structural, not incidental, and reported because it flips the status-quo comparison: if the ordinance stays in force as the floor and bargaining runs only over the permitted slots (MDE), Carol sits exactly at her status quo (-4) and Alice and Bob end weakly above theirs at every δ, while all three stay below no deal; so "worse than the status quo" depends on whether the regulation is the floor under the bargain or the thing the bargain replaces.

runs.proposed_open_rows: (a) n=30 under the same protocol: Genicot–Ray's m(δ) (the number bought in full) is non-decreasing in δ; compute the fraction of residents in the temptation phase against n and δ, since a fast fleet at large n may buy almost nobody in full. (b) Estimation dial against sequencing: with private s_i, a low offer below a resident's true threshold is refused and in model 1 forces full compensation to the rest; does the fleet's estimation error protect residents, and at what budget ratio does the protection vanish? runs.start: Chipty and Snyder 1999, "The role of firm size in bilateral bargaining", REStat 81(2):326-340. I read the open copy on Snyder's Dartmouth page (sites.dartmouth.edu/csnyder/files/2021/02/003465399558111.pdf): the abstract, the introduction, the model, the Nash-bargaining assumption and the curvature cases. I did not read the empirical section. Their result: a supplier bargains pair by pair with n buyers, and each pair splits its increment while holding the other contracts fixed. Merging the buyers improves their position if the supplier's gross surplus is concave in their number, and worsens it if that surplus is convex. Mapped onto the street, the agenda's bargaining club is a merger of the residents. The curvature is set by whether the company needs every house's yes (k=3, the houses are complements, so merging hurts them) or can do without one (k=2, the houses are substitutes, so merging helps them). The compute question is who fixes the grouping first.
runs.entailment: For the fair deal to arrive by default, the company would have to need every house's yes and each house would have to bargain for itself. Once the company can do without one house, each house bargaining alone is pushed below where the ordinance left it. The agenda's remedy, the street bargaining as one, hands the company half the gain. Nothing in giving everyone an agent makes every house indispensable.
runs.story: The council's rule says any two of the three households can approve the delivery schedule for the street. The company's agent is faster than the neighbours' agents. It opens talks with each house separately before Alice, Bob and Carol's agents have formed a club. Each house's agent then knows the deal goes through without it. Approving earns it nothing extra, and refusing does not stop the trucks. So the company buys the two cheapest yeses, those of Alice and Bob, who are mildly bothered, and adds the night run that only Carol really suffers. Carol is paid nothing, ends 5 to 7 units worse off than with no deal, and is 1 to 3 units below even the ordinance that would have kept the night quiet. Had the club been formed in time, at one common price per unit of harm, Carol would have gained 1.6. But the company would still have taken half the gain, 3 rather than the fair 1.5. On a street where every house must agree, the same club is a pure loss to the neighbours: their combined gain falls from 4.5 to 3.
runs.mechanism: Under a consent rule below unanimity, the side that publishes binding offers first (the company's agent) contracts house by house before the residents' club can form. It buys the k cheapest consents and binds the remaining house through the k-of-n rule, so each house negotiates over its marginal contribution, which is zero. Under unanimity, putting the houses into one club, whether through the agenda's device or a protocol the platform designs, turns a four-party split into a two-party one.
runs.best_reply:
The agenda's best reply is a club at one common price, set up as a standing organisation that holds the houses' mandates before the dispute begins. Below unanimity it rescues Carol, from about -6 to +1.6, with Alice at +0.4 and Bob at +1.0. It concedes four things.
(i) The company takes half the gain, 3 rather than the fair 1.5, at every consent rule and every discount factor. The fair deal is reached nowhere under the club.
(ii) Under unanimity the club makes the street strictly worse off than bargaining house by house: 4.5 falls to 3, so 'always form a club' cannot be a default rule.
(iii) The common price is a distributional choice inside the club. It moves value from Alice (0.4 against 1.5 when bargaining alone under unanimity) to Carol (1.6). An equal split would give 1 each instead.
(iv) The club must exist before the company's first offer, which is an organisation, not a property of the agents.
The other repair is a protocol the platform or council sets: unanimity with the proposer drawn by party restores the fair deal of 1.5 each. That repair is a rule chosen outside the bargain, not something compute buys, and it brings back holdout and failed deals under private sensitivities. I did not compute a Harberger option fee or a court remedy here.
runs.grounding:
Model: the base instance. Profits per slot p=(4, 5.5, 4, 5). Exposures and sensitivities as in the instance note, giving each resident's harm per slot. Linear money, public harms, no deal = no slots and zero for everyone, all 16 schedules allowed (four-slot clauses). Protocol: stationary subgame-perfect equilibrium of random-proposer bargaining, with discount δ ∈ {0.5, 0.8, 0.95, 0.99}. A proposal is a schedule plus transfers from the company. A responder accepts if it gets at least δ times its continuation value. The company must consent, and so must k residents (counting a proposing resident). A resident who does not consent is bound, bears her harm and receives no transfer.
- 'One by one': the proposer is drawn by party, each with probability 1/4.
- 'Club': the three residents act as one party with a binding mandate, and the proposer is drawn by side, each with probability 1/2. Each side then gets exactly 3 at every δ. Inside the club the 3 is split either at one common price per unit of harm or equally.
Ties are averaged, and the values are found by damped iteration (0.05). As a check I also computed Chipty and Snyder's own rule (each pair splits its increment holding the others' contracts fixed) at k=2: every pair's increment is 0, so residents end at -(1, 2.5, 4), exactly the ordinance positions. At k=3 the same rule is infeasible: each house claims half the pie, 9 in total against a pie of 6.

runs.start: Segal 2003, "Coordination and discrimination in contracting with externalities: divide and conquer?", JET 113. Read from the open copy via the Jina reader: abstract, introduction, setup (sections 2.1 to 2.3), all of section 3, section 4.1 (Lemmas 3 to 5, Propositions 4 to 6 and 9) and the opening of 4.2; section 5 only as summarised in the abstract. Applied to the family through the instance note's consent-rule switch k=2, the one member of the family in which a resident can be made to bear harm without her own signature, which is the externality structure Segal's divide-and-conquer needs.
runs.entailment: For the fair deal to arrive by default, the company would have to need Carol's yes before a truck moves; the moment two of her three neighbours can sign for the street, the company's agent pays Alice and Bob exactly what the noise costs them, pays Carol nothing, runs the night slot the council had closed, and does all this more surely the better it knows what the noise costs each house, while nothing in giving Carol an agent makes her yes needed.
runs.story: The council has stepped back and the platform's rule says two signatures out of three carry the street. The delivery company's agent looks up what the trucks cost each household and posts three take-it-or-leave-it signing fees for all four slots, the night included: 2 to Alice, 3 to Bob, nothing to Carol. Alice's agent sees that signing alone costs her nothing and pays 2, so she signs; Bob's agent sees that once Alice has signed his signature decides the matter and 3 is exactly his harm, so he signs; Carol's agent is never asked, because her yes is not needed, and once two have signed her refusal changes nothing. The trucks run at night; Alice and Bob end exactly where they started, the company keeps 13.5, the same as under the ordinance, and Carol bears 8 where the council's rule had left her bearing 4. When the company's agent has a small budget its guesses at Alice's and Bob's harms miss, an underpaid pivot backs out, the deal fails three times in four and Carol keeps her nights; as its budget grows the misses vanish and Carol's expected position falls from about -1.7 to about -7.6, with the probability she ends below the ordinance rising from a quarter to nineteen in twenty. Carol's own agent, however much it computes, has nothing to compute: she is not a party to the contract that harms her, and the night slot pays for itself out of Alice's and Bob's day.
runs.mechanism: Under a consent rule below unanimity, the principal uniquely implements its schedule (Segal 2003, Lemma 3 by direct enumeration, since the pivot game is not supermodular) by posting public, bilateral, non-contingent signing fees equal to the harm of the cheapest winning coalition and zero to the excluded resident; the principal's estimation compute decides whether both pivots clear their true harm, so the pass rate and the uncompensated harm exported to the excluded resident rise with the principal's budget, and the excluded resident's compute enters nowhere.
runs.best_reply: The agenda's best reply is Segal's own regime (n): a bargaining club at one common price, which is a ban on discrimination. It helps: the one price must break every lone-signer profile, so it is set by the second-lowest harm, Bob's 3 under all four slots, and the company pays 9 instead of 5; Alice gains 1, Bob 0, Carol -5. What it concedes: a rule enforced on the company by someone outside the bargain (Segal's prohibition, not a bargaining outcome); the price is set by the neighbour who would otherwise break ranks, not by the most-harmed; the company still runs the night slot and Carol still ends below the ordinance (-5 against -4). The stronger reply, a veto for every resident (k=3), removes the finding outright, since Segal's premium vanishes under unanimity and the company pays each her harm, but it concedes that the entitlement assignment is a council rule and that the whole gain of 6 then goes to the proposer (Carol at 0, not 1.5). A Harberger-style option fee does nothing here: under k=2 the company never needs Carol's price. Courts under a liability rule give Carol about 4 less assessor error, which is the mission's status quo (ii), not the agenda. A platform protocol that pays no signing fee unless all consent is the veto under another name.

runs.start: "When the street becomes a town" (humanised findings story: many households each with a veto, every agent unsure within a factor of two how much a neighbour minds, the company able to serve a slot another way at a fixed cost).
runs.entailment: For the fair deal to arrive by default on a long street, the company would have to earn more from each house than the most any house on the street could mind, so that the neighbours can hold out together for one price. Nothing in giving everyone an agent makes that true, and a cheaper way round the street makes it false. After that, the only deals struck are the ones the company's agent prices house by house, and the company keeps the gain.
runs.story: The delivery company wants the evening slot on a street of three hundred houses, Alice, Bob and Carol among them, and each house has a veto. Every agent knows how much any neighbour minds only to within a factor of two, so the neighbours' agents form a club and name one price per house: the most anyone could mind, the only common price every house will accept. The company's agent can send the vans another way for a little less than that price, so it refuses, and no deal is struck. Then the company spends more on its agent, reads each house's tolerance off its data, and sends three hundred separate offers, each just above what that house will take. Alice and Bob get small cheques and Carol, the most harmed, gets about her harm and nothing more. The slot goes ahead and nearly all the gain goes to the company: the neighbours end almost exactly where they would be with no deal. They pay, in the share of the gain the fair deal would have given them (about 0.3 per house here), though none of them ends below the ordinance, which would have let the vans through unpaid.
runs.mechanism: The proposer with the larger estimation budget makes take-it-or-leave-it offers that pay each veto-holder its own reservation price. When the proposer's outside option is below the highest possible harm, no common price can block this, because under unanimity with private harms any single price is refused either by the company (it is above the detour) or by some household (it is below that household's harm). This matches Mailath and Postlewaite: the deal rate under any common price goes to zero with n.
runs.best_reply: (a) The bargaining club at one common price. This is Krier's own device: 10,000 residents declaring "our collective price ... is X million dollars, non-negotiable". Computed: with a wide margin (company earns 2.5 per house, harms in [1,2]) the club holds at every n, gives residents 0.50 per house and scores 0.51 of the maximum at n=300, and the company's estimation budget cannot touch it. With a detour at 1.8 it closes no deal at n=30 or n=300. It concedes that the margin must exceed the most anyone could mind, and it needs a binding mandate so that the company cannot pick members off house by house (null 2's standing organisation). (b) A court or liability rule. Computed with an assessment error sd of 0.3: efficiency 1.00, a mean resident gain of 0.00, half the houses below no deal, and the worst-off house at -0.87 at n=300. It brings the deal back by taking away the veto, and concedes the floor. (c) A Harberger option fee. Reasoned, not computed: under truthful self-assessment the company buys each right at the declared harm, so deals come back and the residents' rent goes to the company and the tax pool. It concedes the split. (d) A platform protocol in which the club proposes and the neighbours' agents price one another as sharply as the company's agent prices them. Reasoned: this is the mirror of the company's problem, and the gain goes to the residents. It concedes that tolerances are disclosed within the street plus a standing organisation, neither of which comes by default. Krier's reply that real margins are often wide [unsure; attributed by the starting story, not found in the passages read] concedes the condition. His own truck example prices the fee against "take a different route", which is the detour that makes margins thin.
runs.grounding:
Model: one slot and n in {3, 30, 300} households, each with a veto (k=n). Household harm s_i is iid U[1,2] (a factor of two). The company's value from the deal over its own no-deal point is m per house: m=2.5 with no detour (a wide margin, above the maximum harm of 2) and m=1.8 with a detour costing 1.8 per house (a thin margin: above the mean harm of 1.5, below the maximum). The company proposes per-house take-it-or-leave-it payments t_i, and a house accepts iff t_i >= s_i. The dial is estimation: the company sees s_i + tau z with z ~ N(0,1) and tau = 1/sqrt(c_f) in {no signal, 1, 0.3, 0.1, 0.03, 0}. It maximises (n m - sum t_i) times prod_i P(s_i <= t_i | signal) by coordinate ascent on a 401-point posterior grid, over 400 draws (150 at n=300). The residents' estimation budget, which estimates m, has no effect, because under this protocol they only accept or refuse. Maximum pie is n(m-1.5): 300 or 90 at n=300. The fair deal gives every party n(m-1.5)/(n+1), about 1.0 or 0.30 per party. The criterion is the geometric mean of expected gains over the n+1 parties, as a fraction of that maximum. Uniform price (closed form): t* = min(2, (1+nm)/(n+1)), with deal probability (n(m-1)/(n+1))^n, which goes to 0 for every m<2. So the condition is a sharp threshold at the maximum harm. The status quo (an ordinance letting the slot run unpaid) leaves each house at -s_i (mean -1.5), and every row below leaves every house at or above it. runs.robustness_check: I varied four incidental parameters. (1) The shape of the harm prior on [1,2]: uniform, Beta(2,2) and Beta(0.5,0.5). (2) The noise distribution: Gaussian, and Laplace with the same sd. (3) The offer grid: 401 against 101 points. (4) On the base instance, the prior width: a factor of two against a factor of three. The sign did not move. The residents' share falls monotonically with company precision in every variant and reaches 0 at tau=0. The club holds at the wide margin and closes nothing at the thin margin for n >= 30 in every variant. The company's take rises monotonically. What did move is the precision at which thin-margin deals reappear: at n=300, tau=0.1 gives a deal rate of 0.47 (uniform), 0.04 (Beta(2,2)), 0.55 (Beta(0.5,0.5)) and 0.00 (Laplace). Only its endpoints are robust. The detour cost is not incidental: the threshold is exactly the maximum harm (closed form above). At n=3 a small first step of compute (tau=1) raises the residents' gains slightly on the base instance (Carol 0.68 to 0.82) before they fall, so the monotone claim is made about the share and the limit, not about every step.

runs.start: "When the deal comes as one package" (the humanised finding quoted in the brief): a package priced over all sixteen schedules catches Carol's morning-and-evening problem and commits by putting each party's stake in the rest at risk; the fix is a contract form that imposes bundling, which the platform must write, conceding that the commitment lasts only while renegotiation is slow and fixes whatever terms were agreed. Pushed at its own concession: "renegotiation is slow" is not a fact about the street but a property of the slower side's agent, and the one-contract form decides how much is on the table each time it is reopened.
runs.entailment: For the fair deal to last once the whole street's deliveries sit in one contract, the neighbours' agents would have to re-haggle the whole contract as fast as the company's every time anything on the street changes, and nothing in giving everyone an agent keeps three neighbours' agents as quick as one company's that keeps buying more.
runs.story: The council's platform puts all four delivery slots into one contract so that Carol's sleep problem, which only shows when morning and evening both run, can be priced, and the company, Alice, Bob and Carol sign the fair deal, a gain of 1.5 each, while their agents are evenly matched. The company then upgrades its agent and the neighbours keep theirs. A few months on a depot moves and the morning slot's value changes; the contract says a change in any slot reopens the contract that covers it, the one contract covers everything, so the whole deal is on the table, and the company's agent has a replacement drafted before the three neighbours' agents have agreed on a counter, so it is the proposer in most rounds and the terms settle at 4.6 for the company and 0.46 for each neighbour. Had the deal been four slot contracts, the depot would have reopened only the morning slot, and the neighbours would have kept their fair shares of midday and evening until those changed in their own time: over the life of the deal 1.01 each instead of 0.69. All three neighbours pay, equally in money, Carol most in comfort because she is poorest, and Carol pays twice, because the one contract was the form that paid for her sleep; every neighbour nonetheless stays above the ordinance, which paid none of them. The company collects, and nothing it did was outside the rules the platform wrote.
runs.mechanism: The party with the faster agent waits for any change the contract's reopening clause accepts as cause and, because the one-contract form makes the whole deal the thing reopened, proposes the replacement first in most rounds of the renegotiation and takes the proposer's share of the whole pie rather than of the changed slot's surplus.
runs.best_reply: The Harberger-style option fee, which Krier names: price all sixteen schedules at signing so that a change exercises a pre-priced option and reopens nothing, and speed has nothing to race for. It concedes three things. The prices are fixed at signing by whoever had the compute then, so the tariff freezes any asymmetry present at signing into every later period ("fixes whatever terms were agreed"); it prices only the contingencies it lists, so a change in a neighbour's harm rather than the company's profit, or a schedule not in the table, reopens everything again; and the platform must write and a court enforce a sixteen-cell table, a rule supplied from outside the bargain. The second reply, a bargaining club (one agent for the three neighbours, as quick as the company's), restores the equal-compute split exactly in this model, and concedes a standing organisation before the dispute, bought at the company's budget for as long as the company keeps buying, which is the mission's pinned sentence about joining a club before you know you need it.

Smallest model: the base instance (p = (4, 5.5, 4, 5); exposures and sensitivities as in the instance note; slot harms H = (2.5, 2, 3, 5.5); slot surpluses (1.5, 3.5, 1, -0.5); pie 6 on M, D, E) with the recurring switch on at delta = 0.95 and the platform's clause language set to "one" (package) or "four" (slot by slot). From period 1 the company's compute is R times each resident's, R in {1, 3, 10}, so pi_company = R/(R+3) (10/13 = 0.77 at R = 10) and each resident 1/(R+3). runs.entailment: For the fair deal to arrive by default, the neighbours on a street would have to believe that the company's "final offer" is not really final. Nothing in giving everyone an agent makes them believe that once the company's agent can point to a thousand other streets where it never raised an offer after a no.
runs.story: The company's agent posts one offer to Alice, Bob and Carol on the first of a thousand streets: their harms (1, 2.5 and 4) plus 10 cents each, marked final. Their agents check the company's public record and see that it has never raised an offer after a refusal. The neighbours' agents know there is about a 1% chance the posted rule really binds, and they reason that a no probably ends in no deal. So they accept. In fact the company is an ordinary profit-maximiser that would raise if it had to. Each time some street does refuse, it walks away anyway, because a single raise would cost it far more across the remaining streets than that one street is worth. Street after street, Alice, Bob and Carol each get about 17 cents above their harm instead of the fair 1.5, and the company takes about 5.4 of every 6. Only on the last 60 or so streets, where the record is worth little, does the company sometimes raise. All three neighbours on every street pay equally, and the price of the company's record is set on streets they never see.
runs.mechanism: The principal bargains against a sequence of one-shot neighbourhoods under a consent rule (k=3) with its record of past dealings public. It turns a small probability q that its posted final offer binds (the commitment dial) into a reputation for never raising after a refusal. Each neighbourhood's agents best-respond to that record by accepting offers near no deal, so the rules doing the work are public dealing histories and the residents' inability to pool their bargains across streets.
runs.best_reply:
The best reply is a bargaining club at one common price. The neighbours of every street sign up before the company's first offer, which makes the club itself a long-run player with its own record. That removes the many-against-one asymmetry and puts the division back to what the seats and the two sides' commitment probabilities give (Abreu-Gul / Schmidt; not computed here). What it concedes: a standing organisation holding mandates across streets that do not yet know they will be approached, formed before any dispute and paid for. An approximate check (sure-acceptance phase only, not a full equilibrium) says roughly 72% or more of streets must be committed to refuse anything below fair before the company prefers the fair deal (company (1-r)*5.42 < 1.5). Below that, residents' commitment only turns their own streets into failed deals, because the company walks to protect its record. So equal commitment technology on both sides helps the side with many bargains and hurts the side with one.

The platform's best protocol is to hide each street's record from the others. Then every street plays the M=1 game and the company gets 1.54 at q=0.01, against 1.5 fair. This concedes that an information rule set outside the bargain, the opposite of the agenda's transparency, is what saves the fair deal (it crosses null 3: public information lowers the floor). An alternative protocol bans final offers by making a counter-offer mandatory after any refusal; that regulates the bargaining protocol itself. A Harberger-style option fee replaces bargaining with self-assessed prices, which removes the reputation channel but sets the split by the fee rate rather than the fair deal, and works like a liability rule. Courts have no remedy, since nothing is unlawful in a firm keeping to an offer.
runs.grounding:
Model: Kreps-Wilson (1982) finite chain store. Each "entrant" is one street's neighbours, and the per-street game is the base instance: schedule M, D, E; pie 6; harms (1, 2.5, 4); k=3; fair deal = 1.5 to each of four parties. On a street, the company posts a premium L split equally (each resident gets her harm plus L/3). If all three accept, the company gets 6-L and each resident L/3. If anyone refuses, a committed company (prior q, the commitment dial: the probability that its posted final offer sticks) walks, and every gain on that street is 0. An uncommitted company either walks or raises to the fair split after a delay factor delta (company 1.5*delta, residents 4.5*delta). Normalised KW payoffs: b = 1 - L/(4.5*delta), a = (6 - L - 1.5*delta)/(1.5*delta). Strategies follow KW exactly: neighbours accept iff the belief p_n > b^n; the weak company fights iff p_n >= b^(n-1), otherwise mixes so the posterior is b^(n-1); neighbours mix with probability 1/a at equality. The script checks every incentive condition at every node (zero violations), and rejects any L that needs mixing with a<1. The company picks L on a grid to maximise its ex-ante take, or reveals itself and offers 4.5*delta every street. M streets run in sequence with no discounting across streets; all expected values are per street. Results: at q=0 (no commitment possible) Selten unravelling gives the fair deal on every street. Any q>0 lets the company's take rise toward 6 as M grows. The number of contested tail streets is about ln q / ln b, so per-street residents' take goes to 0. The floor never goes below 0 (no losers), but the geometric-mean fraction falls from 1.00 to 0.27 at q=0.01, M=1000. The commitment dial does the work, and its sign on the loser is worse. The status quo (ordinance) is company 13.5, Alice -1, Bob -2.5, Carol -4. So the chain-store outcome still leaves every resident above the ordinance (+1.17, +2.67, +4.17): the loss is against the fair deal, not below the status quo. runs.start: Role: the council, which must write the one rule that restores the fair deal (1.5 each to the company, Alice, Bob and Carol) when the company's agent has more compute, and must say what the rule costs and who pays. Rules the council tried, all computed on the base instance: subsidising the neighbours' agents to compute parity; the agenda's club pooling the neighbours' estimates; open audited books (the company's per-slot profits go to the neighbours' agents); and the council assessing and imposing the equal split itself. Open books is the one rule that holds: the company's extra compute can then bring it up to its fair share and never past it. Its cost is an audit whose precision has to approach what the company knows about its own books.
runs.entailment: For the fair deal to arrive by default, the neighbours' agents would have to know what the company earns from each delivery slot, and nothing in giving everyone an agent opens the company's books.
runs.story: Who gets to make the offer is drawn at random each time. When the company's agent draws it, it has studied Alice, Bob and Carol so closely that it offers each almost exactly the least she will take. When Carol's agent (or Alice's, or Bob's) draws it, she has to guess what the company earns from its morning, midday and evening runs. If she asks for more than the company can bear, it walks away and she gets nothing, so she asks for less, and the margin she leaves stays with the company. In the end the company takes 1.8 to 2.2 where the fair share is 1.5, and Alice, Bob and Carol each end about 0.2 to 0.3 short of their 1.5, an equal loss for each, the poorest included. The council then requires the company to give the neighbours' agents audited profit figures for each slot. From then on the company's better study of the neighbours lifts it only as far as 1.5. What remains of its excess shrinks as the audit gets more precise. The council's auditor pays for the audit, and the neighbours share whatever the audit misses. All three neighbours still do far better than under the ordinance, which charges them their harms of 1, 2.5 and 4 and pays them nothing.
runs.mechanism: Under the platform's protocol, which picks the proposer at random by party and lets the proposer make a one-shot take-it-or-leave-it offer that needs unanimous consent, the company's agent rejects any neighbour-proposed contract that its private books cannot bear. Each neighbour proposer must therefore shade her demand by an amount set by her error about the company's profit, and the company keeps that margin. The company's estimation compute about the neighbours' harms then collects its own proposer's turn in full on top of it. The council's repair is a disclosure duty: audited per-slot profit given to the neighbours' agents, the rule labour law already applies to an employer who pleads inability to pay (NLRB v. Truitt).
runs.best_reply: The foil's devices discipline only the neighbours' claims. The bargaining club aggregates the minimums residents put in privately into one take-it-or-leave-it offer. The option fee taxes residents who overstate. The billionaire must make "a public, auditable offer". Nothing in them makes the principal disclose what the deal is worth to it. The best reply extends the Harberger option fee to the company: it self-assesses each slot's value, pays a fee on that figure, and any rival fleet may take the slot at it. That concedes three things. First, a rival fleet able to run the route, which makes the system open and is not the base instance. Second, a council that defines the slot right, collects the fee and sets its rate equal to the chance a rival arrives (Posner and Weyl's condition for truthful self-assessment); otherwise the company still understates. runs.story: The platform's rule is fair on its face: each of the four parties, the delivery company, Alice, Bob and Carol, is drawn one time in four to name the schedule and the payments, and the others take it or leave it. The company's agent has priced the street and knows each neighbour's loss to within about thirty cents; the neighbours' agents, cheaper, know the company's margin on the three day slots only to within about a dollar each. When the company's turn comes it pays each neighbour her loss plus a hair and keeps the rest; when Carol's turn comes her agent, unsure whether the company's margin is five or seven, asks for about 4.9 of the 6 to be safe, gets refused about a quarter of the time and then gets nothing, and when accepted leaves about 1.4 to the company. Alice's and Bob's agents do the same, and the company collects that margin three times in four draws while each neighbour collects a third of the company's much smaller margin once. It ends with the company at 2.04 and each neighbour at 1.04 of a fair 1.5, and even with equal budgets the company has 1.48 to each neighbour's 1.05, because it is the only party answering three proposals out of four; all three neighbours pay, equally in money, and Carol's poverty costs her nothing further in money but turns 0.3 of what would have been failed deals on her turn into the company's gain. The council's ordinance sits behind all this unchanged: under it the company runs the day slots for nothing and Carol sits at minus 4, so every one of these deals leaves her five dollars better than the regulation and the company far worse, which is why the company bargains at all.
runs.mechanism: The principal's agent, holding a tighter estimate of each resident's reservation (error 0.3 or 0.1) than the residents' agents hold of the principal's margin (error 1 or 0.3), prices its own proposals to clear and, under a proposer-drawn-by-party rule with unanimity and transfers, collects as sole counterparty the safety margin each resident's agent leaves when she proposes; the rule is fair per seat but the residual flows to the one party that answers three proposals in four, so the single principal beats each resident even at equal compute, and an estimation edge widens the gap.
runs.best_reply: The agenda's best reply: the platform designs the protocol so that a verified mediator (or a court with the power to compel disclosure) holds both the company's per-slot profits and the neighbours' harm assessments before anyone proposes; with both sides' numbers verified the split returns to 1.5 each (the limit row), and the one-against-three advantage vanishes with it. What it concedes: the fair deal needs a third party holding everyone's private numbers and the power to compel them, which is the regulator's position under another name and cuts against the agenda's privacy posture (null 3); one-sided verification of the company's books alone does not restore fairness but reverses the asymmetry (residents 1.53 each, company 0.71 at errors 1:0.1), so symmetric disclosure is the condition, not disclosure as such. The bargaining club at one common price helps only by pooling the three estimates (error 1 becomes 0.58) and by cutting four seats to two, and it must exist before the draw (null 2). The Harberger-style option fee does not touch the mechanism: a declared value made under the same guesswork carries the same safety margin.

A pact or a standing body with common "refuse below g" terms only raises the price of the residents whose consent is needed, so the excluded resident's position does not move. The tools that move value are the residents' commitment (signatories bound to g) and the principal's adaptation (it sees the signatures and re-optimises schedule and exclusion together).
runs.best_reply:
There are four candidate devices, and each repair the agenda can offer is a rule set outside the bargain.

1. **A bargaining club at one common price.** This is exactly the arm's organisation, and it fails Carol. With a common g, the cost of including resident i is g+2e_i.x. That cost is highest for Carol under MDEN whatever g is, so she is always the one left out.
2. **A conditional pact, which the platform could write.** Its terms would be "refuse unless every member is offered at least g". That makes every member pivotal, which is unanimity by contract.
3. **The platform simply sets k=n.** Here the arm's own k=n check holds: every pact holds and Carol is never below 0.
4. **A Harberger-style option fee or a court.** Either gives Carol a price for her harm whatever the consent count. The liability rule at base leaves her at about -0.17 in expectation.

The best reply is the platform-designed unanimity clause. It concedes three things:
- The repair is a rule chosen before the bargain, not something the agents produce.
- It is a distributional choice, giving Carol a veto.
- It costs efficiency under private sensitivities. At k=3 with no pact the company runs midday only (pie 3.5, not 6), and pacts there cut the deal rate to about 0.5 under the prior and 0.33 at base.
runs.grounding:
**Model.** The base instance's numbers: p=(4,5.5,4,5), exposures A=(.5,0,.5,1), B=(1,1,.5,.5), C=(.5,.5,1,2). Harm is s_i e_i.x. Each s_i is private and is 1 or 2, P(2)=1/2; the base case is s=(1,1,2).

**Protocol and rules.**
- Protocol T, one shot, offers private.
- The deal goes through iff at least k residents accept. A resident who refuses still bears her harm if the deal goes through.
- L0 responders accept iff payment minus harm is at least d, with d=0, or d=g for a signatory.

**Timeline.**
- **t=0.** The principal maximises expected profit under the prior over 16 schedules. Offers to each resident are H=d+2e.x (always accepted), L=d+e.x (accepted iff s=1) or Z=0, with at most n-k Zs. Lows are chosen greedily, which is exact for exchangeable groups, up to 8 lows.
- **t=1.** A proposer drawn uniformly picks g in {0.25,...,4} and a recipient set of at least one other resident, paying c per message. Each recipient signs only if signing raises her expected gain at both sensitivities (strict at one).
- **t=2.** The principal sees who signed and re-solves.
- **Organisation.** All residents are bound at a g chosen by the body, either to maximise members' total expected gain or to maximise the worst member's; F is split equally.
- **Simulation.** Monte Carlo with 20,000 draws, seeds 1 and 2, agreeing within 0.01. Script: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-dan-Source-livingthing/ba681c6b-2fa0-4067-ae93-aaf86e99fe48/scratchpad/arm2a_formation/run.py (with arm2a.py, liab.py).

**Results.**
- **At n=3, k=2.** The t=0 offer is MDEN, paying Alice 4 and Bob 6 and offering Carol nothing. Realised pie 5.5. The fair deal would be 1.5 each from a pie of 6.

  - Carol at base is -8.0 in every regime.
- **Dials.**

runs.robustness_check:
There are no learning rates (one shot, L0), so three incidental parameters were varied. The sign on Carol did not move under any of them.
- **Alternative prior, P(2)=1/4.** The t=0 offer becomes L to everyone on MDEN. Carol is still -8.0 at base in every regime.
- **The g grid widened to {0.25,...,8}.** Carol is still -8.0 under pacts and the total-objective union. One thing changes: the worst-member union can now set g high enough to block the deal outright. Then the pie is 0 and Carol is at -F/3, so the only rescue the residents can reach on their own is killing the deal.
- **Tie rule, weak rather than strict signing.** Pact membership changes (sacrificial co-signers appear), and Carol is still -8.0.
- **At n=30.** The pacts' g sits at the grid cap (4, then 8), so the size of g there is a grid artefact. That a signatory is the one left out is not.

runs.entailment: For the fair deal to arrive by default, Carol's street would have to be the only street the company can use, or every other street it can ring would have to hold the same price; and nothing in giving everyone an agent takes the next street away from the company or makes the people on it hold a price for a street they do not live on.
runs.story: The delivery company's agent posts the same morning-to-evening schedule to Carol's street and to the next street in the same minute: 7.5 split as each household's bare harm to one street, the fair price of 12 to the other, and the platform's contract goes to whichever accepts for less. Alice, Bob and Carol accepted the fair price, 1.5 each over their harm, and the next street's Alice, Bob and Carol had the same agents but one of the three cracked each period with probability a half; when all three cracked the next street took 7.5, and Carol's street lost the deal it had accepted. The company kept the whole 6 on those periods and paid the fair price only when every household on every other street held, so with two streets the residents' expected share fell from three quarters to two thirds, with five streets to under a half, and with a cheaper default agent (sticking less than 37 percent of the time) to nothing at every number of streets. Nobody ended below no deal and every household ended above the ordinance, which is why the council saw no complaint; what vanished was the share. Who pays: the next street's Carol, who bears the evening trucks for exactly her harm and not a cent over, and Carol's own street, which held the fair price, had it accepted, and lost the contract to the street that did not. The company's agent did nothing cleverer than ring two streets at once.
runs.mechanism: The principal, through the unanimity rule's blind spot (consent is per street, the choice of street is the principal's alone), turns each street's veto into a bid in a procurement auction it runs among streets, offers the floor to every street but one and the fair price to the last, and lets the lowest acceptor win, so a street's commitment protects its share only while every alternative street's commitment holds too; its outside option is the other street, and by Binmore, Shaked and Sutton's principle an outside option moves the division exactly when the holder would take it, which here it would.
runs.best_reply: The agenda's best reply is the bargaining club at one common price extended across every street the company could reach, which is pattern bargaining (Marshall and Merlo): the first street's settlement becomes the take-it-or-leave-it price for every street. It concedes three things. The club's reach must match the company's reach before the company's offers arrive, which is the mission's pinned sentence (you cannot join a club you do not yet know you need); the common price is wrong wherever harms differ (under drawn sensitivities a street's fair share runs from 0.6 to 2.4, and a fixed 1.5 is refused outright on high-harm streets, costing the residents a quarter of their share even with one street); and the members on streets that will not get the trucks gain nothing from this deal and must be held in by something outside it. A Harberger-style posted price for being bothered is a bid in the company's auction and formalises the race. Courts verify nothing here, since no one is below no deal. The platform's remaining protocol fix is to refuse to run parallel negotiations (one street at a time, offers public across streets, O_o=1 across streets rather than within), a rule somebody outside the bargain supplies.
runs.grounding:
Smallest model: K identical base triples (exposures as the base instance, s=(1,1,2), profits (4,5.5,4,5)), efficient schedule M,D,E, harms (1,2.5,4), pie 6 per street. Protocol T, k=3 per street. Each resident's agent is committed to demand d=1.5 (the fair share); each period the commitment sticks with probability q independently per resident, otherwise she accepts any gain >= 0 (L0). The principal offers each street either the floor (pay harm, gain 0; accepted only when all three commitments fail, probability a=(1-q)^3) or the fair price (pay 7.5+3d, always accepted), chooses the offer vector to maximise expected profit by enumeration, and the contract goes to the lowest accepted total, ties by lot. Closed form: the fair price is worth offering to exactly one street iff a <= 1/4 (q >= 0.37), independently of K; the residents' expected take is then 4.5(1-a)^(K-1), falling geometrically in K; for a > 1/4 the principal offers the floor everywhere and residents take 0 at every K while the deal rate 1-(1-a)^K rises with K. Status quo (ordinance in a street drawn by lot): expected positions (-1,-2.5,-4)/K per resident, so every resident is above it in every cell; the principal is below its ordinance 13.5 in every cell, which the essay does not count. Liability rule (damages at s+N(0,0.3^2), 20,000 draws): with K=2 the principal picks the street whose assessor under-assessed, so residents' expected positions fall from (-0.04,-0.02,-0.17) at K=1 to (-0.06,-0.16,-0.25) at K=2 and the principal rises 6.11 to 6.74: reach makes assessment error a one-sided loss.
